claim: If f is continuous on [a,b] and F is any antiderivative of f, then ∫_a^b f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a).
conceptual_move: The theorem provides a powerful computational shortcut: instead of summing infinitesimal areas, one can find an antiderivative of the integrand and evaluate it at the endpoints. This transforms the problem of integration into one of antidifferentiation.

explanation: This card records a modern textbook presentation, not a reconstruction of either Newton’s or Leibniz’s independent original formulation. The proof of Part 2 uses a regular partition of [a,b] and telescopes the differences F(x_i) - F(x_{i-1}) to express F(b) - F(a) as a sum. By the Mean Value Theorem, each difference equals f(c_i)Δx for some c_i in [x_{i-1}, x_i]. Substituting and taking the limit as n approaches infinity, the sum becomes the Riemann sum that defines the definite integral. This establishes the equality. The theorem is also known as the evaluation theorem because it allows direct evaluation of definite integrals. It relies on the existence of an antiderivative, which is guaranteed by Part 1 for continuous functions. The choice of antiderivative is irrelevant because any constant of integration cancels out in the subtraction F(b) - F(a). This result is a cornerstone of calculus, enabling practical computations in physics, engineering, and economics.
limits: The theorem requires continuity of f; it may fail for functions with discontinuities
It requires finding an antiderivative, which may not be expressible in elementary functions
The result gives the net signed area, not the geometric area, which can be negative if the function is below the x-axis
Independent original formulations require separate primary-source records; they have not been reconstructed here.
problem: Computing definite integrals directly from Riemann sums or geometric formulas is extremely cumbersome and often impractical for complex functions. A more efficient method was needed to evaluate integrals exactly.
scientific_standing: Established theorem, central to calculus, universally accepted.
source_evidence_role: Source-grounded account; consult attribution notes for original versus secondary evidence.
title: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part 2: evaluation of definite integrals via antiderivatives
